title: Recognise and address poultry production-related problems observed, at

lessons.title: Spotting problems early
lessons.html:
Spotting problems early

Most production problems in poultry show small warning signs before they become disasters. A worker who knows what normal looks like can spot the change and act quickly.

Use your senses on every walk

  • Look: bird distribution, activity, posture, feathers, droppings, litter, feeders and drinkers.
  • Listen: normal soft sounds versus coughing, rattling, loud distress calls or unusual silence.
  • Smell: ammonia makes eyes sting; a musty smell may mean mouldy feed or wet litter.
  • Feel: air temperature and draughts at bird height; litter moisture in your hand; crop fill in chicks.

Use the numbers

NumberWarning sign
Daily deathsHigher than the previous days or normal for the age
Water useDrop or sudden rise compared with yesterday
Feed useLower than standard for the age
Bird weightsBelow the breed standard, or uneven flock
Egg numbersDrop in production, more cracked or soft-shelled eggs
TemperatureOutside the set range, big swings day to night

A drop in water intake is often the first sign of trouble - sometimes a day before birds look sick.

Record and compare

Write down what you see and the numbers each day, so you can compare with yesterday and with the standard. A problem is easier to solve when you know when it started.

Look at the whole house

Walk the full length of the house and look at both sides, the corners, near the fans and near the doors. Problems often start in one area, such as a cold corner or a leaking drinker line. Comparing different parts of the house helps you find where a problem began and what may have caused it.

lessons.title: Common problems and their likely causes
lessons.html:
Common problems and their likely causes

Problem observedPossible causesFirst actions
Chicks huddling, slow startHouse too cold, draughts, cold floorCheck heaters, curtains, inlets; report
Birds panting, wings spreadHeat stress, poor ventilation, power failureCheck fans, cooling, water; report urgently
Wet, caked litterLeaking drinkers, high water pressure, poor ventilation, diarrhoeaFix leaks, adjust drinkers, replace wet litter, report
Strong ammonia smellWet litter, too little ventilationReport; supervisor adjusts ventilation
Low water useBlocked lines, air locks, pump problem, sick birdsCheck lines and nipples; report
Uneven flock, small birdsPoor brooding, feeder or drinker space, diseaseCheck equipment heights and space; report
Lame birdsLeg disorders, wet litter, infectionsReport; cull suffering birds as trained
Feather pecking (layers)Bright light, crowding, nutrition, boredomRemove injured birds; report
Drop in eggs, poor shellsDisease, heat, feed, light programme fault, waterCheck lights, water, feed; report
More floor eggsNests not attractive, dark corners, nest accessCollect often; report
Sudden high deathsDisease (possibly avian influenza or Newcastle disease), heat, power or water failureReport immediately to the manager; move nothing

Think about more than one cause

Problems often have more than one cause. Wet litter, for example, may come from drinkers, ventilation and disease all together. Check the simple things first: water, feed, air, temperature and light.

Equipment problems

Many bird problems start with equipment: a stuck feeder auger, a blocked water filter, a broken fan belt, a failed heater or an inlet that will not open. When birds behave strangely, check the equipment in that area. Report faults to maintenance at once and write them on the house card.

lessons.title: Taking action and following up
lessons.html:
Taking action and following up

A simple problem-solving method

  1. Observe: what exactly is wrong, where in the house, how many birds, since when?
  2. Check the basics: feed, water, air, temperature, light, litter, equipment.
  3. Act within your authority: fix a leak, unblock a drinker line, lower a feeder, remove dead and wet litter, close a door that causes a draught.
  4. Report to the supervisor: what you saw, numbers, what you did.
  5. Record it on the house card.
  6. Follow up: check again later. Did the action work? Are birds behaving normally?

Know your limits

Some actions need the supervisor, manager or vet: changing controller settings, giving medicine, changing feed, culling large numbers, or deciding on disease. Do not guess with medicines or settings. Report quickly so the right person can act.

Emergencies

  • Power failure: check the generator has started; raise the alarm; follow the farm's emergency plan.
  • Water failure: report at once; birds suffer quickly without water, especially in heat.
  • Fire: raise the alarm, get people out, call for help; do not put yourself in danger.
  • Suspected controlled disease: report immediately; the manager must contact the state vet under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; stop movements.

Welfare

Birds that are badly injured, very sick or cannot reach feed and water must be culled humanely by a trained person without delay, as required by the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Learning from problems

After a problem is solved, discuss it with your supervisor and team. What warning signs came first? What could prevent it next time? This builds your skill in recognising problems early.

Key points

  • Use your senses and the daily numbers to spot problems early.
  • A drop in water intake is often the first warning sign.
  • Check feed, water, air, temperature, light and litter first.
  • Act within your authority, report and record, then follow up.
  • Report sudden high deaths immediately and move nothing.
